Recently I was asked a question that I haven’t been able to get out of my head: “In light of all that has changed, what are the things that you used to argue were true, that you no longer believe?” For those that aren’t familiar with my work, I’m not focused on the latest framework or process or tool.  Instead, I’m interested in the underlying principles .   The things that form the foundation of strong product work, and that stay true despite constant changes.   And the real test of that is whether the content I wrote 20 years ago, and 10 years ago, is still relevant today. That said, given the transformative nature of AI, I think it’s very fair to question everything, even principles I’ve long considered sacred, and to try to honestly tackle that question. Realize that I treat my content as my product, and literally every week I am doing product discovery on my content.  So there’s been a lot of learning. I want to talk about what I consider my most serious mistakes and regrets; the kind of things that I desperately wish I understood earlier in my career. I decided to draw the line at the publication of the first edition of INSPIRED, published in 2008.  I wrote this book after 25 years of learning and practicing the craft of product, at both an individual contributor level and a product leadership level, at some of the leading companies of the time. So what follows are what I consider the ten biggest things I’ve learned since then, that represent a significant change from what I had publicly argued in my content … 1. Business Viability There’s no getting around it.  I completely understated the importance of business viability.   In fact, in the first edition, the product risks were only value, usability, and feasibility , and viability was buried under feasibility.  In the second edition of INSPIRED, published 10 years later, viability did become its own risk, but literally hundreds of thousands of product people heard from me this very one-sided view of the product role. While business knowledge has always been valuable, today, especially when working on AI products with very challenging viability risks related to costs, monetization, liability, and ethics, it’s increasingly essential knowledge for product people. I’ve thought a lot about how I could have misunderstood the role in such a fundamental way, and I believe the reason was because nearly all of my career up until then was building developer tools and platforms, which is one of the rare places that you can actually get away with weak business skills , and very limited knowledge of viability.   And if you have a product-inclined engineering lead, which I was, you often don’t even need a product manager. More generally, I have always been grateful for my engineering training and experience that I brought to the product role. I never believed that was the only path, but I have always believed it unlocked so much, and it still helps me to quickly learn and apply new technologies. While those are valuable skills, going forward, I think the real superpower is a deep understanding of business viability – especially from a systems thinking perspective. 2. Problem Discovery I’ve always emphasized that product discovery has elements of problem discovery and solution discovery , and there are good techniques for each, but I simply didn’t understand how strongly people would be drawn to the problem discovery side of the equation , and end up viewing themselves as gatekeepers for determining if they have a problem worth solving, and leave themselves too little time for solution discovery. Many product people go further down this path and obsess over whether this is “the most important problem” for us to solve – which is actually a fruitless and unanswerable question.  All we can know for sure is that this is a real problem that’s worth solving. Yes, it should be pretty obvious that we need to understand the problem to be solved, who we’re solving that problem for, and what success looks like for the business. But whether enough people have this problem, and wish it could be solved, is rarely hard, and not where the real work is. When a product fails, it’s almost always because the solution the team came up with just wasn’t good enough. You might think a product failed because not enough customers have the problem, but as soon as someone else comes along with a better solution, suddenly it’s embarrassingly clear what the real issue was. Whatever the reason, so many product people spend way too much time questioning and validating the problem, and then, once they finally end up agreeing, they think their big contribution is to explain the reason this is a problem to the rest of the product team , which leads to the next issue… 3.
